units.translation: Who could cast out the accursed offspring from the house?
accursed (fem. gen. sg. or acc. pl.)

From this stem, of which one example exists in Homer (Od. 14, 25) and one in Theocritus (25, 103), or from ἄρω [to fit], of which no examples are found, two tenses of the middle form are derived: the perfect ἄρηρα [I have fitted] (which the tragedians consistently said as ἄραρα [I have fitted], preferring the Doric a to the Ionic n as in many other words) and the second aorist ἤραρον [I fitted], used with the same meaning as ἤρεσα [I pleased], the aorist of the verb ἀρέσκω [I please, I am agreeable]. Aeschylus used only the perfect ἀραρέναι [to have been fitted], i.e. to be fixed or made firm.

where ὀμώμαται γὰρ ὅρκος [for the oath has been sworn] was read, which I corrected from Cramer's Anecdota Oxoniensia vol. 1 p. 88, 8 and the Vossian codex of the Etymologicum Magnum p. 134, 35, where the verb ἀρηρέναι [to have been fitted] is discussed and the verse, with the poet's name omitted, is cited thus: ἄραρε γὰρ ὅρκος ἐκ θεῶν μέγας [for a great oath from the gods has been fixed].

You lie in the spider's web.
